2 Machine Learning for cancer classification Which new skill do you want to learn and why? I want to learn how to apply Machine Learning to biological data using R. I already have experience with R and RNA-seq data analysis, but Machine Learning is a completely new skill for me. Since I want to further develop my skills in bioinformatics and computational biology, I would like to learn how algorithms can recognise patterns and make predictions. How are you going to learn this skill and what is your plan? With 32 hours available for this project, my plan is as follows: Activity Time Machine Learning theory and fundamentals 4 hours Learning to work with tidymodels 5 hours Finding and exploring a dataset 3 hours Data preprocessing 5 hours Applying Random Forest 6 hours Evaluating and comparing models 5 hours Reporting the results 4 hours Total 32 hours How are you going to demonstrate that you have mastered this skill? I want to use a publicly available gene expression dataset to answer the following research question: “Can machine learning algorithms distinguish between healthy and COVID-19-affected tissue based on gene expression data?” The final product will be a self-written R Markdown document in which I present the code, data processing, visualisations, results and conclusions. This will demonstrate that I can independently process a dataset, apply machine learning and correctly interpret the results. 2.1 Importing Packages and Data In this step, we load the required packages and import the gene expression data from GEO dataset GSE152641. library(edgeR) library(randomForest) library(caret) library(pROC) library(AnnotationDbi) library(org.Hs.eg.db) library(ggplot2) # Import count data filepath <- "data/GSE152641_Inflammatix_COVID19_counts_entrez.csv.gz" covid19_exp <- read.csv(gzfile(filepath), check.names = FALSE) # Create count matrix counts <- as.matrix(covid19_exp[, -1]) rownames(counts) <- as.character(covid19_exp[[1]]) storage.mode(counts) <- "numeric" # Check dimensions dim(counts) ## [1] 20460 86 2.2 Retrieving Metadata and Groups In this step, we retrieve the metadata from GEO. This allows us to determine which samples originate from COVID-19 patients and which are healthy controls. # Read metadata geo <- readLines("data/GSE152641_family.soft") # Find sample names and disease groups sample_names <- grep("!Sample_title", geo, value = TRUE) groups <- grep("disease:", geo, value = TRUE) # Remove unnecessary text sample_names <- sub("!Sample_title = ", "", sample_names) groups <- sub(".*disease: ", "", groups) # Combine information samples <- data.frame( sample = sample_names, group = groups) # Match samples with count data samples <- samples[match(colnames(counts), samples$sample), ] # Show group distribution table(samples$group) ## ## COVID19 Healthy control ## 62 24 2.3 Data Quality Checks We check whether the expression matrix and metadata have been imported correctly and matched with each other. # Check whether sample names match all(colnames(counts) == samples$sample) ## [1] TRUE # Check missing group information sum(is.na(samples$group)) ## [1] 0 # Check number of samples per group table(samples$group) ## ## COVID19 Healthy control ## 62 24 2.4 Data Filtering and Normalisation We first split the data and filter genes exclusively based on the training set. # Set a seed to ensure reproducible results set.seed(123) # Convert the sample groups into a factor outcome <- factor(samples$group) # Split the data into 80% training and 20% testing train_index <- createDataPartition(outcome, p = 0.8, list = FALSE) # Filter genes using only the training samples keep <- filterByExpr(DGEList(counts = counts[, train_index], group = outcome[train_index])) # Keep the selected genes in all samples y <- DGEList(counts = counts[keep, ]) # Use a training sample as the reference for TMM normalization y <- calcNormFactors(y, method = "TMM", refColumn = train_index[1]) # Convert counts to logCPM and transpose the matrix expression <- t(cpm(y, log = TRUE)) # Show the number of samples and genes after filtering dim(expression) ## [1] 86 15282 # Prepare training and test sets x_train <- expression[train_index, ] x_test <- expression[-train_index, ] y_train <- outcome[train_index] y_test <- outcome[-train_index] 2.5 Training the Random Forest Model We check the distribution of the training & test sets and then train the Random Forest model. # Check training and test sets dim(x_train) ## [1] 70 15282 dim(x_test) ## [1] 16 15282 table(y_train) ## y_train ## COVID19 Healthy control ## 50 20 table(y_test) ## y_test ## COVID19 Healthy control ## 12 4 # Train Random Forest model set.seed(123) rf_model <- randomForest(x = x_train, y = y_train, ntree = 500, importance = TRUE) rf_model ## ## Call: ## randomForest(x = x_train, y = y_train, ntree = 500, importance = TRUE) ## Type of random forest: classification ## Number of trees: 500 ## No. of variables tried at each split: 123 ## ## OOB estimate of error rate: 7.14% ## Confusion matrix: ## COVID19 Healthy control class.error ## COVID19 48 2 0.04 ## Healthy control 3 17 0.15 2.6 Evaluating the Model on the Test Set We test how well the model can distinguish between COVID-19 patients and healthy controls using data it’s never seen before. # Predict the groups of the test samples predictions <- predict(rf_model, newdata = x_test) # Compare predicted groups with actual groups confusionMatrix(predictions, y_test, positive = "COVID19") ## Confusion Matrix and Statistics ## ## Reference ## Prediction COVID19 Healthy control ## COVID19 12 1 ## Healthy control 0 3 ## ## Accuracy : 0.9375 ## 95% CI : (0.6977, 0.9984) ## No Information Rate : 0.75 ## P-Value [Acc > NIR] : 0.06348 ## ## Kappa : 0.8182 ## ## Mcnemar's Test P-Value : 1.00000 ## ## Sensitivity : 1.0000 ## Specificity : 0.7500 ## Pos Pred Value : 0.9231 ## Neg Pred Value : 1.0000 ## Prevalence : 0.7500 ## Detection Rate : 0.7500 ## Detection Prevalence : 0.8125 ## Balanced Accuracy : 0.8750 ## ## 'Positive' Class : COVID19 ## 2.7 Calculating the ROC Curve and AUC We evaluate the model’s ability to distinguish between the groups using the ROC curve and AUC. # Calculate probabilities probabilities <- predict(rf_model, x_test, type = "prob")[, "COVID19"] # Calculate ROC curve roc_model <- roc(y_test, probabilities, levels = c("Healthy control", "COVID19")) # Calculate AUC auc(roc_model) ## Area under the curve: 0.9792 # Plot ROC curve plot(roc_model, main = "ROC Curve - Random Forest", col = "blue", print.auc = TRUE) 2.8 Identifying and Visualising the Most Important Genes We identify the ten most important genes based on Mean Decrease Gini, convert the Entrez Gene IDs into gene symbols and visualise the results. # Calculate gene importance gene_importance <- as.data.frame(importance(rf_model)) # Select top 10 genes top_genes <- head(gene_importance[order(gene_importance$MeanDecreaseGini, decreasing = TRUE), ], 10) # Convert Entrez IDs to gene symbols top_genes$SYMBOL <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, keys = rownames(top_genes), column = "SYMBOL", keytype = "ENTREZID", multiVals = "first") # Plot top 10 most important genes ggplot(top_genes, aes(reorder(SYMBOL, MeanDecreaseGini), MeanDecreaseGini)) + geom_col() + coord_flip() + labs(title = "Top 10 most important genes", x = "Gene", y = "Mean Decrease Gini") + theme_minimal() 2.9 Discussion This study investigated whether a Random Forest model could distinguish between COVID-19 patients and healthy controls based on gene expression profiles from bulk RNA-seq data. The model achieved an accuracy of 93.75% and an AUC of 0.9792. This indicates that the model was able to distinguish pretty well between the two groups within this dataset. The sensitivity was 100%, meaning that all COVID-19 patients in the test set were correctly classified. The specificity was 75%: three out of four healthy controls were correctly classified. One healthy control was incorrectly predicted as a COVID-19 patient. However, the results should be interpreted with caution due to the limited size of the test set. It consisted of only 16 samples, including 12 COVID-19 patients and 4 healthy controls. As a result, one incorrectly classified sample can have a relatively large impact on the performance metrics. Furthermore, the model was evaluated on samples from the same dataset used for training. External validation using an independent dataset is therefore necessary to determine whether the model also performs well on other patient groups. In addition, the ten most important genes were selected based on Mean Decrease Gini. This measure indicates which genes were important for the predictions made by the Random Forest model. However, this does not automatically mean that these genes are specific biomarkers for COVID-19. Further research is needed to investigate their biological relevance. 2.10 Conclusion The Random Forest model was able to distinguish between COVID-19 patients and healthy controls based on bulk RNA-seq gene expression data. The model achieved an accuracy of 93.75% and an AUC of 0.9792, indicating strong classification performance within the dataset used. These results demonstrate that Random Forest can be a promising method for classifying COVID-19 based on gene expression profiles. However, due to the small test set and the lack of external validation, it cannot yet be concluded that the model can be reliably applied to new, independent patient groups.

4 Reproducible Science 4.1 Reproducing a data analysis 4.2 Assessing reproducibility

4 Reproducible Science In this section, I demonstrate my understanding of reproducible science through two assignments. First, I reproduce a data analysis using C. elegans data. Second, I assess the reproducibility of a published scientific article and attempt to reproduce its R code. 4.1 Reproducing a data analysis 4.1.1 Data import First, I import the dataset using the readxl package. data <- read_excel("data/CE.LIQ.FLOW.062_Tidydata.xlsx", sheet = "expParameters") 4.1.2 Data inspection I inspect the first rows and the structure of the dataset to check whether the data has been imported correctly and whether the variables have the correct data types. head(data) ## # A tibble: 6 × 34 ## plateRow plateColumn vialNr dropCode expType expReplicate expName ## <lgl> <lgl> <dbl> <chr> <chr> <dbl> <chr> ## 1 NA NA 1 a experiment 3 CE.LIQ.FLOW.062 ## 2 NA NA 1 b experiment 3 CE.LIQ.FLOW.062 ## 3 NA NA 1 c experiment 3 CE.LIQ.FLOW.062 ## 4 NA NA 1 d experiment 3 CE.LIQ.FLOW.062 ## 5 NA NA 1 e experiment 3 CE.LIQ.FLOW.062 ## 6 NA NA 2 a experiment 3 CE.LIQ.FLOW.062 ## # ℹ 27 more variables: expDate <dttm>, expResearcher <chr>, expTime <dbl>, ## # expUnit <chr>, expVolumeCounted <dbl>, RawData <dbl>, compCASRN <chr>, ## # compName <chr>, compConcentration <chr>, compUnit <chr>, ## # compDelivery <chr>, compVehicle <chr>, elegansStrain <chr>, ## # elegansInput <dbl>, bacterialStrain <chr>, bacterialTreatment <chr>, ## # bacterialOD600 <dbl>, bacterialConcX <dbl>, bacterialVolume <dbl>, ## # bacterialVolUnit <chr>, incubationVial <chr>, incubationVolume <dbl>, … 4.1.3 Scatterplot of the raw data I create a scatterplot to visualise the relationship between chemical concentration and the number of offspring. Different colours represent the chemicals, while different shapes represent the experimental conditions. data$compConcentration <- as.numeric(data$compConcentration) ggplot(data, aes( x = compConcentration, y = RawData, colour = compName, shape = expType)) + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0.5), alpha = 0.7) + scale_x_log10() + labs(x = "Concentration (log10)", y = "RawData", colour = "Chemical", shape = "Experiment type") + theme_bw() 4.1.4 Data normalisation I normalise the data using the mean of the negative control. This makes the mean value of the negative control equal to 1, expressing all other measurements as a fraction of this value. negative_mean <- mean(data$RawData[data$expType == "controlNegative"], na.rm = TRUE) data$normalised <- data$RawData / negative_mean mean(data$normalised[data$expType == "controlNegative"], na.rm = TRUE) ## [1] 1 4.1.5 Scatterplot of the normalised data I create a second scatterplot to visualise the normalised measurements. ggplot(data, aes(x = compConcentration, y = normalised, colour = compName, shape = expType)) + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0.01), alpha = 0.7) + scale_x_log10() + labs(x = "Concentration (log10)", y = "Normalised RawData", colour = "Chemical", shape = "Experiment type") + theme_bw() 4.1.6 Explanation of the analysis The negative control in this experiment is S-medium without added chemicals. This serves as a baseline to measure normal reproduction. The positive control is ethanol and is used to check whether the experiment can detect a particular effect. The negative control represents the normal situation. The positive control demonstrates whether the experiment can detect an effect. The vehicle control checks whether the solvent itself influences the results. Normalisation ensures that the mean of the negative control equals 1. This allows all other measurements to be compared fairly with the normal situation. 4.1.7 Plan for further research: dose-response analysis For further research, a dose-response analysis could be performed to determine the IC50 using the drc R package. Install the drc package. Select a chemical and use its corresponding concentrations and measurements. Fit a dose-response model using a log-logistic model. Visualise the dose-response curve. Calculate the IC50 concentration. 4.2 Assessing reproducibility 4.2.1 Article Marinos et al. (2020). Defining the nutritional input for genome-scale metabolic models: A roadmap. Article | GitHub repository 4.2.2 Research question How can the nutritional composition of a growth medium be accurately translated into input data for genome-scale metabolic models? 4.2.3 Methods and results The researchers developed a roadmap using E. coli and LB medium. They used R to analyse the nutritional composition and predict bacterial growth. The results show that different nutrients, such as amino acids and carbohydrates, influence the predicted growth. 4.2.4 Transparency criteria Criterion Assessment Explanation Study Purpose Yes The research objective is clearly described. Data Availability Statement Yes A separate statement about data availability is provided. Data Location GitHub Data and R scripts are available on GitHub. Study Location No No specific location is mentioned. Author Review Yes The authors provide their email addresses. Ethics Statement No No separate ethics statement is included. Funding Statement Yes Funding from the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft is mentioned. Code Availability Yes The R scripts are publicly available on GitHub. 4.2.5 Reviewing the R code Code description The R code uses a metabolic model of E. coli to investigate how nutrients influence predicted bacterial growth. Flux Balance Analysis is used for this purpose. The code calculates the effects of additional nutrients and visualises the results using bar plots. Readability Score: 3/5 The code contains clear comments and is organised into sections. However, some functions and calculations are too complex for me to fully understand. I also had to adjust the file paths several times. Reproducibility Score: 2/5 I attempted to run the analysis in RStudio, but encountered installation problems with glpkAPI. As a result, I was unable to reproduce the figures. Although the code and data are publicly available, the analysis requires adjustments before it can be executed successfully.

5 SQL 5.1 Loading the datasets 5.2 Checking and making the datasets tidy 5.3 Standardizing country and date variables 5.4 Checking country names 5.5 Preparing the datasets for joining 5.6 Saving the datasets 5.7 Importing and joining the datasets using SQL 5.8 Visualizing the joined data 5.9 Conclusion

5 SQL 5.1 Loading the datasets We load the dengue and flu datasets from local CSV files. The Gapminder dataset is loaded from the dslabs package. library(tidyverse) library(dslabs) dengue <- read_csv("data/dengue_data.csv", skip = 11) flu <- read_csv("data/flu_data.csv", skip = 11) gapminder_data <- gapminder 5.2 Checking and making the datasets tidy The dengue and flu datasets are initially stored in wide format, with each country represented by a separate column. We transform these datasets into long format using pivot_longer(). dengue_tidy <- dengue %>% pivot_longer(cols = -Date, names_to = "country", values_to = "dengue") flu_tidy <- flu %>% pivot_longer(cols = -Date,names_to = "country", values_to = "flu") The Gapminder dataset is already in tidy format. 5.3 Standardizing country and date variables The dengue and flu datasets contain weekly dates, while Gapminder contains yearly data. We standardize the country and year variables to make the datasets compatible for joining. dengue_tidy <- dengue_tidy %>% mutate(country = as.character(country), year = as.integer(substr(Date, 1, 4))) flu_tidy <- flu_tidy %>% mutate(country = as.character(country), year = as.integer(substr(Date, 1, 4))) gapminder_tidy <- gapminder_data %>% mutate(country = as.character(country)) The datasets now have matching data types for country and year. 5.4 Checking country names The country names were checked across all three datasets using unique(). The datasets contain different numbers of countries, but four countries are present in all three: Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Mexico. 5.5 Preparing the datasets for joining Only countries present in all three datasets are selected. The weekly dengue and flu data are summarized into yearly averages to match the yearly Gapminder data. # Select countries present in all three datasets common_countries <- unique(dengue_tidy$country[ dengue_tidy$country %in% flu_tidy$country & dengue_tidy$country %in% gapminder_tidy$country]) # Filter all datasets dengue_tidy <- dengue_tidy %>% filter(country %in% common_countries) flu_tidy <- flu_tidy %>% filter(country %in% common_countries) gapminder_tidy <- gapminder_tidy %>% filter(country %in% common_countries) # Calculate yearly averages dengue_yearly <- dengue_tidy %>% group_by(country, year) %>% summarise(dengue = mean(dengue, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") flu_yearly <- flu_tidy %>% group_by(country, year) %>% summarise(flu = mean(flu, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") The dengue and flu datasets now contain yearly averages for each country. This allows them to be joined with Gapminder using country and year. 5.6 Saving the datasets The three prepared datasets are saved as CSV files so they can be imported into PostgreSQL. write_csv(dengue_yearly, "data/dengue_yearly.csv") write_csv(flu_yearly, "data/flu_yearly.csv") write_csv(gapminder_tidy, "data/gapminder.csv") 5.7 Importing and joining the datasets using SQL The three CSV files were imported into the PostgreSQL database workflowsdb using DBeaver. Each dataset was stored in a separate table: dengue_yearly, flu_yearly and gapminder. We used SQL queries to inspect the tables and combine the datasets using INNER JOIN, matching records based on the shared country and year variables. SELECT * FROM dengue_yearly AS dengue INNER JOIN flu_yearly AS flu ON dengue.country = flu.country AND dengue.year = flu.year INNER JOIN gapminder AS gapminder ON dengue.country = gapminder.country AND dengue.year = gapminder.year; 5.8 Visualizing the joined data We load the joined dataset exported from PostgreSQL as a CSV file and visualize the yearly dengue and flu data for the four countries. Two separate line graphs are created to show how dengue and flu values change over time. joined_data <- read_csv("data/joined_data.csv") # Dengue ggplot(joined_data, aes(x = year, y = dengue, color = country)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + labs(title = "Dengue over time", x = "Year", y = "Average dengue") + theme_minimal() # Flu ggplot(joined_data, aes(x = year, y = flu, color = country)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + labs(title = "Flu over time", x = "Year", y = "Average flu") + theme_minimal() 5.9 Conclusion The datasets were successfully combined using PostgreSQL and imported into R for visualization. The line graphs show how dengue and flu values change over time across the selected countries. This assignment helped me gain experience with importing, manipulating and combining datasets using SQL and R. I also learned how to use the joined data to create visualizations.

6 R Package 6.1 Introduction For this assignment, I developed my own R package: cleanDataTools. The goal of this assignment was to learn how to create an R package and make it available to others through GitHub. I chose to develop a package containing simple functions for checking and cleaning datasets. During data analysis, it is important to first assess the quality of a dataset. Missing values and duplicate observations, for example, can affect further analyses and their results. With cleanDataTools, I aim to combine several commonly used data cleaning operations into a single package, allowing me to reuse these functions in future analyses. 6.2 Functions My package contains four self-written functions. Each function is stored in a .R file in the directory. Function Description count_missing() Counts the number of missing values (NA) in each column. remove_missing() Removes rows containing one or more missing values. count_duplicates() Counts the number of duplicate rows in a dataset. remove_duplicates() Removes duplicate rows while keeping the first occurrence. These functions help check and clean datasets before they are used for further analysis. 6.3 Package structure During the development of the package, I used the R packages usethis and devtools. These packages allowed me to set up the structure of my own package and manage its different components. The structure of my package looks as follows: The main components are: DESCRIPTION: Contains information about the package, such as its name, version, author and description. R: Contains the four separate files with my functions. man: Contains the documentation for the functions. NAMESPACE: Determines which functions are made available to package users. tests: Contains tests that I used to check whether the functions work correctly. vignettes: Contains explanations and examples of how to use the package. 6.4 Documentation For the documentation of my functions, I used roxygen2 comments. These describe, among other things, the parameters, output and examples of the functions. I then used the devtools::document() command to generate the documentation files and the NAMESPACE file. 6.5 Testing To check whether my functions work correctly, I wrote a test for each of the functions using testthat. The tests check, among other things, whether missing values are counted correctly, duplicate rows are removed and the correct number of duplicate rows is reported. When running devtools::test(), all four tests passed. 6.6 Vignette I also added a vignette explaining what the package does and how the different functions can be used. The vignette includes examples that allow users to try out the functions themselves. I checked whether the vignette was available using: browseVignettes("cleanDataTools") 6.7 Publishing on GitHub As the final step, I published my package in a public GitHub repository. This allows others to view my code and install the package themselves. The package can be installed directly from R using: devtools::install_github("davalyn/cleanDataTools") After installation, the package can be loaded using: library(cleanDataTools) I tested the installation myself and then ran all four functions again. All functions produced the expected results. GitHub-repository: cleanDataTools 6.8 Reflection During this assignment, I learned how an R package is structured and which components are needed to make custom functions available to others in an organised way. Working with separate function files, roxygen2 documentation and testing functions was particularly educational. I also learned how GitHub can be used to share code and how a package can be installed directly from a repository. An important insight is that creating reusable functions is not only convenient for personal use but also contributes to reproducible research. By documenting functions and combining them into a package, the same steps can be performed consistently across different analyses. In the future, I can further expand cleanDataTools by adding additional data cleaning functions. This will allow me to continue using and improving the package in future data analyses.
